title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Liam Chen
body:
Purpose

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and ADRs. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers designing services and models to be deployed on Redwood's hosted, dedicated, and private platforms.

Scope

Applies to: all backend services, model-serving components, and infra IaC owned by Redwood product and platform teams. Does NOT apply to one-off research notebooks or vendor-managed SaaS integrations unless explicitly adopted.

Principles (short)

- Design for production: predictable latency, cost visibility, and operational simplicity.
- API-first and backwards-compatible: explicit versioning + deprecation policy.
- Observability by default: every service ships metrics, traces, and structured logs.
- Security and least privilege: secrets, RBAC, and network segmentation enforced.
- Small blast radius: isolation via routing, model variants, and rollback policies.

Section 1: API Standards

Overview
APIs are the primary integration surface for customers and internal services. Follow REST/JSON for synchronous endpoints and gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs unless the use-case needs streaming (use server-sent events or HTTP/2 streaming).

Key rules
1. Naming and Resources
   - Use plural resource nouns: /v1/models, /v1/inference-requests.
   - Use kebab-case for path segments and snake_case for JSON keys.
2. Versioning and Compatibility
   - Every public endpoint must include a major version: /v1/.
   - Semantic compatibility: non-breaking additions allowed in minor releases; breaking changes require a new major version and 30-day beta rollout.
3. Authentication & Authorization
   - All public APIs require token-based auth (Bearer tokens). Internally, use mTLS + service identity.
   - Respect RBAC policies for model access and audit logging.
4. Error Handling
   - Use consistent HTTP codes and structured error payloads: {"code":"invalid_input","message":"...","details":{}}.
   - Include correlation_id in errors for tracing.
5. Pagination & Filtering
   - Cursor-based pagination for large lists: {"next_cursor":"..."}. Limit defaults: 50, max: 1000.
6. Rate limiting & Quotas
   - Client-facing endpoints should return 429 with Retry-After when rate limited. Include headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
7. Streaming & Partial Responses
   - For long-running generation, support HTTP chunked streaming and an async jobs API (/v1/jobs). Provide progress updates via events.
8. Contract testing
   - New endpoints must include OpenAPI spec checked into the service repo and run contract tests against the mock gateway in CI.

Examples (curl)
- Synchronous generation:
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"prompt":"Hello"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

Section 2: Coding Standards

Languages and runtime choices
- Primary backend languages: Go (services), Python (model adapters, evals), Rust/C++ for high-performance runtime components.
- All code must target maintained language versions (Go 1.21+, Python 3.11+).

Style and linting
- Use company's style guides: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/mypy for Python. CI must fail on style violations.
- Enforce type hints for Python public modules.

Testing and quality gates
- Unit tests: >= 80% coverage for core logic.
- Integration tests: exercise API contract and main code paths.
- End-to-end tests: smoke tests against staging; model-serving integration tests for latency/accuracy.
- All PRs > 200 LOC require at least two reviewers including one owner-team reviewer.

CI/CD
- Every repo must have standardized CI workflows that run linters, tests, and security scans. Deployments gated by pipeline checks.

Secrets and keys
- No secrets in repo. Use Vault/KMS for secrets. Use ephemeral credentials where possible.

Section 3: Infrastructure Standards

IaC and provisioning
- Terraform is the canonical IaC. Keep modules in terraform-modules repo. Use remote state with locking.
- PRs that change infra require runbook and cost estimate.

Networking and security
- Default deny network posture. Use Transit VPCs for cross-account networking.
- Enforce subnets: public (load balancers), private (services), mgmt (bastion/ops).

Instance & GPU policies
- Use instance families pinned per workload. For model-serving: NVIDIA A10/A100 or equivalent; record AMI/driver/containers in infra manifests.
- Tagging policy: team, cost_center, env, service.

Backups and DR
- Critical configs have daily backups with 30-day retention. RTO/RPOs must be documented for each service.

Cost controls
- All infra changes must include cost delta estimate. Use autoscaling and right-sizing guidelines from Optimize team.

Section 4: Model-serving Standards

Model packaging and artifact registry
- Models are packaged as versioned artifacts with metadata (architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, expected memory/kv-cache needs). Store in the model-registry (S3 + manifest).

Versioning and rollout
- Semantic model versions. Canary deploys: start at 1% traffic for 1 hour, then 10% for 6 hours, then ramp to 100% if no regressions. Provide automatic rollback on SLO violations or quality regressions.

Quantization & profiles
- Maintain quantization_profiles per model (e.g., int8-q4, fp16). Profiles include expected token throughput and memory delta. The runtime consults profiles to select kernels.

Serving runtime expectations
- Implement KV cache management, continuous batching, and prefix caching. Models must expose recommended max_sequence_length, batch_size, and preferred kernels in the manifest.

Fallbacks and variants
- Define compatible model variants for graceful degradation (e.g., fp16 fallback when int8 missing). Routing rules should prefer lower-cost variants for background tasks.

Model validation and evals
- Every model must pass a pre-serve validation suite: correctness smoke tests, performance benchmarks (latency, memory), and evals against canonical prompt sets. Record results in the eval-harness dashboard.

Section 5: Observability Standards

Metrics
- Use Prometheus-compatible metrics and standard labels: service, env, region, model_version, route. Export these from both service and runtime.
- Mandatory metrics for all services: request_count, request_latency_seconds (histogram), error_count, token_count (for model-serving).

Tracing
- Use OpenTelemetry for traces. All incoming requests must carry a trace context. Correlate logs and traces via trace_id.

Logging
- Structured JSON logs with fields: ts, level, service, env, msg, correlation_id, extra. Log levels: debug/info/warn/error. Avoid PII and raw prompts in logs; use hashed prompt IDs when needed.

Dashboards & Alerts
- Every service must publish a per-service dashboard (latency, errors, throughput, cost) and SLO dashboard. Alerts template:
  - P99 latency > target for 15m -> P2 page to oncall.
  - Error rate > baseline by 3x for 5m -> P1 alert.

Retention & compliance
- Metrics: 90 days. Logs: 30 days by default; customer-sensitive logs follow retention rules in security-and-compliance.

Section 6: Performance Standards

SLOs and targets (examples)
- Public inference endpoints (hosted API): p95 <= 250ms for short prompts (<128 tokens); p99 <= 900ms.
- Dedicated model-serving internal RPCs: p95 <= 150ms, p99 <= 500ms.
- Throughput: document expected tokens/sec per GPU profile in model manifest.

Capacity planning & load testing
- Services must have capacity targets (sustained QPS and burst QPS). Run load tests before major releases using benchmark-runner in staging.

Profiling and performance playbook
- Use flamegraphs, per-kernel telemetry, and allocation tracing. The profiling-playbook in eng-serving-runtime has step-by-step instructions for collecting:
  1) Reproduce load in perf cluster.
  2) Capture perf counters and kernel traces.
  3) Identify hot paths and submit a performance ADR if a long-lived change is required.

Section 7: ADRs (Decision Records)

Format and process
- Use ADR format: title, status, context, decision, consequences, date, owners. Store ADRs under architecture-and-standards and link them from relevant repos.

Recent decisions (examples)
- 2025-09-12: "Default to int8 quantization for large encoder-decoder models" — motivated by cost/latency tradeoffs; rollback plan defined.
- 2026-01-18: "Adopt OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing" — added tracing sidecar baseline.
- 2026-02-20: "Unified API versioning approach" — standardized major-version pathing and deprecation windows.

How to create an ADR
1. Draft ADR in docs/adr/<repo> with template.
2. Get reviewers (architecture guild + owner).
3. Publish and link in this page.

Section 8: Governance & Ownership

Owners
- Architecture & Standards lead: eng-arch@redwood.ai (primary steward).
- Each service must have an on-call owner and a documented owner_team in service metadata.

Review cadence
- Standards reviewed quarterly by architecture guild. Major infra or API changes require an ADR and a cross-team review.

Change and rollout checklist (mandatory for infra or public API changes)
1. Create design doc and ADR (if decision-level).
2. Cost & security review.
3. Test plan and rollback runbook.
4. Staged rollout with canary percentages and SLO-monitoring.
5. Post-rollout review and update docs.

Templates and snippets

- OpenAPI snippet (example):
  openapi: 3.0.1
  info:
    title: Redwood Generate API
    version: 1.0.0
  paths:
    /v1/generate:
      post:
        summary: Generate text
        responses:
          '200':
            description: OK

- Example model manifest (YAML):
  id: gptx-7b
  version: 2026-02-01
  architecture: decoder-only
  quantization_profiles: ["fp16", "int8-q4"]
  recommended_max_seq: 4096
  expected_gpu: a10

Appendix: SLO and Threshold Table

- Hosted API (short prompts <128 tokens): p95 250ms, p99 900ms, availability 99.9% monthly.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): p95 150ms, p99 500ms, availability 99.95% monthly.
- Model-onboarding validation: accuracy/regression tests pass rate 100% on baseline prompt-set; perf within 10% of expected.
